title: Elephants Become Last Lifeline in Flood-Ravaged Arunachal Pradesh as Crisis Deepens Across 26 Districts
excerpt: With roads destroyed and bridges swept away, authorities have deployed elephants to transport fuel and helicopters to airlift rice to cut-off communities in India's northeast.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over one lakh residents affected by floods across 26 districts in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Seven fatalities reported due to flash floods and landslides in the region.
  • Elephants are transporting diesel fuel to aid in debris clearance operations.
  • 11.5 metric tonnes of rice airlifted to cut-off communities in Lower Siang district.
  • Heavy rainfall warnings continue as the crisis deepens in the region.

  • At least seven people have been killed and over one lakh residents affected by flash floods and landslides across 26 districts in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Elephants have been deployed to transport diesel fuel for earth-moving machines in areas where no road access remains.
  • The Indian Air Force and state helicopters airlifted 11.5 metric tonnes of rice to the cut-off Koyu circle in Lower Siang district.
  • The India Meteorological Department has warned of continued heavy rainfall across the region.

When Only Elephants Can Get Through

In the remote Lower Siang district of Arunachal Pradesh, where weeks of monsoon fury have destroyed every road and bridge linking communities to the outside world, two elephants are doing what no truck, helicopter, or military vehicle can. They are hauling drums of high-speed diesel through wrecked jungle trails to reach earth-moving machines stationed at Koyu headquarters — the only equipment that can begin clearing the debris choking the region's lifelines.

The image has become a defining symbol of India's northeast flood crisis, now in its fourth week. Flash floods and landslides have killed at least seven people and affected more than one lakh residents across 26 of Arunachal Pradesh's 28 districts, according to state disaster management authorities. Entire villages remain cut off. National Highway 13, a critical artery connecting several districts, is blocked by landslides at multiple points.

"In one operation, 11.5 metric tonnes of rice — 230 bags — were transported in four sorties from Pasighat to Koyu."

Airlifts and Rescue Operations

The Arunachal Pradesh government has launched emergency helicopter operations, using a state-leased Skyone MI-172 helicopter to airlift supplies. In one operation, 11.5 metric tonnes of rice — 230 bags — were transported in four sorties from Pasighat to Koyu. Stranded passengers from Ziro, Daporijo, and Koloriang were evacuated in separate sorties.

The Indian Air Force has joined rescue operations, deploying helicopters for damage assessment and survivor searches. The National Disaster Response Force and State Disaster Response Force teams are conducting rescue operations across multiple districts, though the terrain and continuing rain have hampered access to several affected areas.

In Lower Dibang Valley, nine people went missing after the Sisiri River overflowed. A rescue operation suffered a major setback when an inflatable rubber boat carrying seven crew members and three rescued individuals was swept away by strong currents. Three elephants were subsequently deployed to locate stranded residents in areas inaccessible by any other means.

A State Overwhelmed

The scale of destruction is staggering for a state with a population of roughly 1.7 million. Flash floods triggered by the overflowing of the Siang, Subansiri, and Sisiri rivers have flattened homes, destroyed farmland, and severed road and telecommunications links. In Keyi Panyor district, the death toll reached three after a body was recovered from neighboring Papum Pare district, carried downstream by floodwaters.

Chief Minister Pema Khandu said disaster management policies "must be tailor-made to suit regional terrain," acknowledging that standard infrastructure approaches cannot serve the mountainous, heavily forested landscape of India's northeastern frontier. The state has sought additional central assistance as the Indian Meteorological Department warned of more heavy rainfall across the region in the coming days.

A Recurring Crisis

Recurring Flood Challenges
›Arunachal Pradesh faces severe flooding every monsoon season.
›Current disaster among the worst in recent years.
›Climate change intensifying rainfall patterns in the region.
›Infrastructure gaps hinder disaster response efforts.

Arunachal Pradesh, India's largest northeastern state by area, faces catastrophic flooding nearly every monsoon season, but the current disaster is among the worst in recent years in terms of geographic spread. Climate scientists have noted that the Himalayan region is experiencing more intense and erratic rainfall patterns, with glacial lake outburst risks adding a new dimension to the annual monsoon threat.

For the communities now relying on elephants and helicopters for their most basic supplies, the crisis underscores a persistent gap: India's remote border regions remain desperately underserved by the infrastructure needed to respond to disasters that are becoming more frequent and more severe.
